Paper_name: Exploring the influence of self-identification on perceptual judgments of physical and social causality
Summary: This research examined whether self-identification with a geometric shape (established via a shape-label matching task, Sui et al. 2012) influences perceptual judgments of physical and social causality. In two experiments (each N = 64 students), participants first learned arbitrary associations between their own identity ('you') and a geometric shape (circle/square) and between a stranger's identity and another shape. A matching task administered after the learning phase confirmed a robust self-prioritisation effect (faster and more accurate responses when the label 'you' was paired with the self-related shape). The main task presented animations in which the self-related shape and the stranger-related shape took agent/patient roles in causal interactions, with the identity-role association counterbalanced across two blocks; participants rated perceived causality ('How much did you cause the motion of the stranger?'). Experiment 1 showed that physical causality ratings were shaped solely by kinematic cues; Experiment 2 (emphasising social causality) confirmed the dominance of kinematic parameters, with a negligible impact of the identity manipulation.
Author: Michele Vicovaro, Francesca Squadrelli Saraceno, Mario Dalmaso
Conclusion: Contrary to the hypothesis that self-identification would diminish causality ratings under specific identity-role associations, the matching task confirmed a robust self-prioritisation effect (successful shape-label association) while physical and social causality judgments were dominated by kinematic cues, with negligible impact of the identity manipulation.
